name: 'Auf ibn al-Ahwas
bio: 'Auf ibn al-Ahwas was the son of the chief of 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah who commanded at Shi'b Jabalah (in or about A.D. 570), and himself one of the captains that day. He was grandfather of 'Alqamah ibn 'Ulathah, the rival of 'Amir ibn at-Tufail.
Lyall describes Ode XXXVI as a collection of fragments, wanting both beginning and end.

poems.title: Ode XXXV: The cisterns have been broken down
poems.author: 'Auf ibn al-Ahwas
poems.note: Lyall's heading: 'Auf son of al-Ahwas, of Ja'far ibn Kilab, of 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah.
poems.text:
The cisterns have been broken down, and there is not left to one of them of its coping-stones so much as the stone on which the bucket from the well is poured forth.

Khaulah's were they when her people halted there, and my folk and hers dwelt there together, facing each the other.

Now is it hard to trace the outlines of a dwelling-place, and that which the blaze has spared of the sticks of firewood.

I swear by Him to whose sacred precincts Quraish go on pilgrimage, and that which Mount Hira gathers together [of offerings],

And by the holy month of the Sons of Umayyah, and the victims when they are bound [for sacrifice] with the blood soaking into the ground where they stand —

I will never blame thee so long as tears roll down from mine eyes : if I do, then may God wipe me out of being !

I acknowledge your authority as long as life lasts, and I accept it, even though it should bring the loss of all my goods ;

Do not therefore show crookedness in your judgement of set design, even as the wood of the sara-tree is naturally crooked ;

And I will not attempt, in dealing with you, to conceal the truth, so as to make the judgement vain, even as a contest of cleverness is a vain thing.

But as for thee, Son of Kalb, thy sitting in judgement upon me would be the same as the wrapping of me in my shroud for burial !

Take ye Da'b [my son] as a hostage for the damage I have inflicted upon you — ye have no superiority over Da'b :

For among those not of royal race none has superiority over us ; and ye can find an equivalent for your slain man among [us,] your friends and kinsmen.

Hast thou any kinship with the race of Hujr son of 'Amr, which thou knowest and I know not ?

Or with al-'Anqa, Tha'labah son of 'Amr— the blood of these is a cure for dog-madness ?

And I think not that ye be kings of the race of Nasr — kings have a very high price !

But I have gained glory from the side of father and mother both, and my high place reaches up to both of them.

Thine ancestors were Bujayyid and the man Ka'b ; and thou didst no wrong in taking what thou wouldst ;

But a people from the root of Qais — their payments [as bloodwit] are camels and herdsmen therewith ;

And [War] is pierced, when I gain mastery over her, even as a piece of broiling meat is pierced by the skewer or spit,

By a spear with a sharpened head of which I thrust into her a long iron point, the knots in which are athirst for blood.

poems.title: Ode XXXVI: Many the wanderer, causing my dogs
poems.author: 'Auf ibn al-Ahwas
poems.note: Lyall's heading: The same. Lyall describes this as a collection of fragments, wanting both beginning and end.
poems.text:
Many the wanderer, causing my dogs to bark, who fears the lonely desert, while before him are the twin portals and curtains of the darkness of night,

To whom I have raised my beacon-fire, and when he had guided his steps thereby, I have chidden my dogs, that no biter among them should snarl at him.

Ask not me, but enquire [from others] regarding my disposition, what time those who seek to the pot are so many that they turn away him who desires to borrow it,

And they sit round about it watching it [till it be cooked] ; and the cherished maiden of the tribe is among those who kindled its cooking-fire :

Then shalt thou see that my pot does not cease to be, to the frozen wanderer wrapped in a furry skin, as it were a mother to whom he comes for comfort —

Open for all to see : never is a curtain set before it ; when other-fires are extinguished, its message of welcome shines bright.

When the milkless camels come home at night from the pasture, and redeem not their flesh by means of their milk, the barren one among them tastes the spear-point.

As for me, I drop every cause of quarrel the beginning of which makes its appearance on the part of my cousin, and I am careful not to stir it up,

For fear lest its rancour should bring evil things to pass : and verily great events are stirred up by very little things.

When evil speech is spoken, I make over the hearing of it to other ears than mine, and I ask not concerning it what the object of it is.

Suraim bring their sheep from Julajil to me ; and between us is Dhat Kahf and its rugged and lofty table-lands.

Why have ye wreaked your vengeance on sons and lords, whose breasts were free from all rancour against you ?

'Twas they raised you [by their glorious deeds] to heaven ; and nearly had ye attained thereto, if ever mortal man gained access to it.

Kings were they, though their salutation was that of subjects ; as for their oaths and their vows, they were always fulfilled.

And if the son of Zahr and his kindred be not of my stock, nevertheless Riyah are of my kin, their good and their ill ;

And Ka'b — verily I am the son of the tribe and their sworn friend, and their helper whensoever they are hard pressed in strife.

By thy life ! on the Day of 'Unaizah I should have lighted on my heart's desire, if only its purpose had held firm in my soul :

But it is the destruction of a man's affairs if he do not twist them firm : and there is no good in one who twists a rope who does not twist it hard.
